utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Meek. Yes, that's it. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Mitchell. I can't see behind. Is that all? Yes. Mr. Zivanovic, I see you're pretty much crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Here on my right is our legal assistant, Mr. Djordje Kalanj. He's an attorney at law from Belgrade. Here is also Mr. Petar Vuga. He's our expert for military and security issues. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So welcome, Mr. Vuga. Also present are the following Defence experts; Mr. Trifunovic for the Borovcanin Defence team. Good morning, Mr. Trifunovic. General Kosovac for the Miletic Defence team. Good morning, General. Admiral Antic for the Pandurevic Defence team. Good morning, Admiral. Are you named after the famous footballer, because I remember a footballer famous by that name from your country. He passed away, I understand, didn't he? Anyway, let's start. Good morning to you, sir. Welcome back. I hope you had time to rest. We have a long journey ahead, which we have barely started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, yesterday, we left off -- we had just -- you had talked about a law that regulated MUP forces in combat with the army; and in looking -- we're now looking at a -- at a document that I just started reading to you, and I'll try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is 65 -- or Exhibit number 4D00087.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is from the Drina Corps Command, from the deputy assistant commander for logistics, Colonel Ljubo Sobot, and it is to the Main Staff, as we see in the upper left-hand corner. It's entitled: "Requesting Food Provisions for a MUP Unit Monitoring the Srebrenica and Bratunac Enclaves." It says: "Among others, a MUP unit comprising 400 policemen has been engaged to monitor the Srebrenica and Bratunac area. We have been informed that their engagement and, consequently, food supplies for them have been arranged through the Main Staff, rather than organs and sources of the civilian authorities of the RS and Bratunac municipality." Then it asks for some direction: "Please advise who is in charge of the food supplies. Is it the Drina Corps or the brigade," and it goes on asking for advice from the Main Staff. Can you relate this document in any way to any of the provisions that we'd just seen in the previous law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes, Madame Fauveau. I wasn't sure if you were standing or not, actually. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's always the same thing. There's always a part of a sentence which we don't have, and I think the whole sentence must appear. It's not only the brigade of the Drina Corps but also the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madame Fauveau. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't read the whole document. I didn't think it was necessary. I don't understand the point she's making. I mean, I can read it, if she wants me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's read it. It will speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Everyone's looking at it, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a short document, it's on the record, we see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the problem with this document is precisely to know whether it is a civilian organ or the army who are in charge of the food for the police. I think the presentation made by the Prosecutor ignores this point in this document. I'm not asking for him to read the whole document, but he can't present the document, saying whether it is the brigade or the corps. It has to be all the organs mentioned by the corps directly, and in particular the municipality organs of Bratunac, and also the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree it's asking about that as well. That's not something I was trying to cover up. I think we can all see that in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, anyway, the point has been made. Mr. Butler has the document in front of him. He knows what the point is; he knows what your question is. If he wants to move from the military to the municipality or to the Ministry, he's free to do so, I mean, always depending on his personal assessment, knowledge, and assessment of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, having in mind the whole document, not just my synopsis of it, of course, can you relate it to the previous law we saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is a reflection of the part of the law on the use of the RS MUP in this nature, that when they're put under military command, it's incumbent on the military to provide them with the necessary logistics. That would include food, that would include ammunition, that would include other forms of life support. So this particular document, you know, reflects that manifestation of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move -- oh, one other area related to regs or policies. Can you tell us, in the beginning - very briefly - the JNA, was there a concept for the corps related to the zone of responsibility? In the corps rules, was there a concept laid out regarding the corps zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the original rules of the JNA, they don't define -- yeah, it's explicitly what's known as a corps area of responsibility. The JNA was designed to fight as a modern military force on the battlefield, not necessarily as the way that the VRS, you know, fought on a more geographical basis and the Republika Srpska and how the units were organised. So you don't have a direct -- a direct collateral between the JNA doctrine and what the VRS ultimately used, which was areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about did the JNA talk about the areas of responsibility or zones of responsibility for brigade units in the original material that you're talking about from the 1980s?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back and actually look at that. I believe the answer is, no, that the brigade rules don't specifically delineate that as -- as an area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How about the VRS in the wartime period? Did you -- the Court has seen many documents that talk about a zone of responsibility, and we'll see some. But in your opinion, was there such a thing as a zone of responsibility for the brigades?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much of it traces its origin back to the fact that most of the brigades of the VRS, not only within the Drina Corps but in other areas of the country as well, were initially organised and supported with respect to soldiers from that area, funding from that area, by the individual municipalities. So what happened as the army matured was that these particular brigades, not only were they given the names of particular municipalities, but when you look at the VRS map graphics, you'll note that they have designated areas or zones of responsibilities that, more often than not, correspond with the geographical boundaries of the various municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now moving on to just some of the principal documents that you've cited in your Main Staff report and you've discussed over the years, let's go to 65 ter 2739, which should be in your mixed binder volume 2, tab 1. It's a document from the 5th Corps Command, dated 12 May 1992, and it's referencing a decree of the SFRJ, and talks about General Mladic assuming command. Can you just tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the documents originated by 5th Corps to the commander and commands to inform them that based on the order from above, in this case the SFRY Presidency, noting that Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic has been appointed to the position of Chief of Staff and concurrently the deputy commander of the 2nd Military District, which was then the highest JNA formation in Bosnia, headquartered in Sarajevo. It also lists, as part of that same degree, assignments of General Gvero, General Djukic, and Colonel Tolimir within the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document you've talked about. It should be the next on your list, and it's 65 ter number 25. This is the minutes of the 16th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, also dated 12 May 1992. If we go to page 2 in the English, item 6, it mentions that the Assembly unanimously elected Karadzic, Vlasic, and Kojovic as members of the Presidency of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If we go on to item 8, it says: "The Assembly unanimously adopted the decision on establishing the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Army. Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic was appointed the commander of the SRBH Army Main Staff." How does that relate to the previous document, which appears to be dated the same?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The former -- or the former JNA 2nd Military District ultimately became the nucleus for what would later become the VRS Main Staff. So, I mean, I believe some other witnesses, I believe Colonel -- I mean, Colonel-General Milovanovic, testified previously about some of the timing issues related to this. But there was an awareness particularly with respect to this Assembly meeting, that those JNA officers who were being appointed to the 2nd Military District were, in fact, going to be designated as the senior leadership figures of the newly-organised Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to -- you've also, in this document, in your reports, cited to -- mentioned something called the six strategic objectives, which we have put, in part, in paragraph 19 of the indictment. I believe you cite to what is English page 13 of this document, B/C/S page 12. I believe it's Karadzic saying, I think in the third paragraph: "The Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Presidency, the Government, the Council for National Security which we have set up have formulated strategic priorities; that is to say, the strategic goals for the Serbian people. The first such goal is separation from the other two national communities-separation of states." Then it goes on to say: "Separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century, to attack us, and who would continue with such practices if we were to continue to stay together in the same state." It talks about the second strategic goal which we did not mention in the indictment, and then it mentions the third strategic goal on the next page. It's B/C/S 13: "The third goal is to establish a corridor in the Drina Valley, that is, the elimination of the Drina as the border between the two worlds. We and our strategic interest and our living space are on both sides of the Drina. We now see a possibility for some Muslim municipalities to be set up along the Drina as enclaves in order for them to achieve their rights, but it must basically belong to Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina. "That belt along the Drina which, as much as it is strategically useful for us in a positive way, helps us by damaging the interests of our enemy to achieve their goal of gaining a corridor with which would connect them to the Muslim International and render this area permanently unstable." Mr. Butler, the -- the six strategic objectives referred to in the indictment, especially the two that are in the indictment, how do these comments relate to what we have put in the indictment? Are they the same or different?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I believe, and I won't bring it up, but the formal document regarding the six strategic objectives is dated 1993. Do you know how that -- we have this Assembly in 1992 and then they come out in 1993. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that while the actual strategic objectives were articulated in May 1992, for whatever reason the Government of the Republika Srpska did not decide to publish those in their own Official Gazettes until 1993. I don't know the exact reasons why they elected to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to another document you've talked about. It's dated back in 1992. It's tab 3, 65 ter 29. This is a document that has been brought up several times, I believe. It's from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, dated 19 November 1992. It says: "Very Urgent: "Directive for further operations of the Army of Republika Srpska to the commander (Chief of Staff) personally. Directive operational number four." It's in the name of Commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic and drafted by Major-General Manojlo Milovanovic. Now, Mr. Butler, you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think there is a mistake in the transcription, because the Serbian version does not say "personal," which has been mentioned in the English version, after the commander and the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we can look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not in a position to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have the CLSS translation, and it says "personally," but I don't know where that came from. There may be another version of the document out there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the meaning of the first two words, "na licnost."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Personally."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Personally" is what I just heard the interpreter tell us. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move. But thank you for raising the matter. The only two words that I had doubts upon were precisely, "na licnost." So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, did this document help you in your analysis of looking into the intentions of the RS and the VRS towards the areas of Srebrenica, Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- you have -- and, first of all, can you tell us, it says it's a directive. Can you tell us what a directive is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At various times during the conflict, either keyed to a perceived change in the political environment or a perceived change in the larger or broader strategic goals of the nation, the Main Staff of the Army drafted, for their leadership, a series of what are known as these operational directives. I believe there are a total of nine of them published through either the course of the war or through the course of the war and then the month beyond to begin the first transition into the postwar environment. I believe the OTP has approximately seven of the nine. These documents essentially lay out what the I would call the strategic direction of the army in how it's going to, in broad terms, fulfill the political objectives that had been mandated by the political leadership of the Republika Srpska. So in the first part of the war, you see a number of these, 1 through 4. In the second several years of the war, where the objectives do not change radically, you see far fewer of these. Then by March of 1995, you see publications of further directives in order to deal with new, changing situations on the political and military front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And as the Court has seen, in this document, laying out some of the background, it says, on page 3 of the English: "I have decided the following," and then it starts listing various corps, giving them their directives. Let's go to the Drina Corps section, which is page 5, in the English it should be, and B/C/S, page 11, entitled "The Drina Corps." It says, in section D: "The Drina Corps. From its present positions, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad (the dam), Zvornik and the corridor; while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas." Now, I'm going to stop there for a minute. Is there anything, in your view, illegal or improper, militarily, about that statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. If you were to stop there, there would be nothing wrong with it, as far as I could tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But it goes on and says: "... together with the Muslim population." Now, I don't need you to get into a long discussion about that; but in your view, what is that statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it - you know, I don't believe, I'm certain in fact - it fundamentally defines the character of the campaign to follow; that is, objective becomes, in part, the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you, and, again, just briefly, at the time that this was written, 19 November, can you just give us a little historical background in the -- in the -- what was happening in this area, Naser Oric's forces, how they were doing, and what, if anything, this is responding to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In keeping in line with the earlier strategic directives, the key priorities for the Army of the Republika Srpska at the time pertained to areas with respect to the Krajina; Bijeljina; the Posavina corridor; Sarajevo; and to a lesser extent, Hercegovina; and then, finally, the area of the Drina Valley. Until the beginning of November 1992, that particular area, the Podrinje and Drina River area, did not have its own dedicated corps. In fact, that territory was split up between a number of corps courses, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the East Bosnia Corps. It was recognised strategically to be important; but with the forces on hand and the other objectives that the army needed to acquire, it was not their top priority. Beginning, as a result, by November of 1992, the Muslims were in a far stronger military position in that particular area than certainly the VRS was comfortable with. There were active Muslim military forces in the Kamenica, Cerska, Bihac area which greatly threatened communications particularly between Zvornik, Vlasenica, Sekovici, and those key areas. Large forces were in south of that area under the command of Naser Oric, who, of course, was expending his territory at the expense of the forces in the area of Bratunac; and as history would show, a month and a half later, was literally at the gates of the town of Bratunac itself. So while ignoring this particular area, in light of more important objectives nationally, the VRS recognised that it got itself into a significantly adverse situation with respect to the Muslim military forces, and this directive is the first mark -- you know, mark in the sand, along with the establishment of the Drina Corps, that it was time for the VRS to begin to focus a higher priority on this region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in November of 1992, do you know where Vinko Pandurevic was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to this period, up through October 1992, then Captain First Class Pandurevic was the commander of the Visegrad Light Infantry Brigade. Sometime, I believe it's approximately 14 October, he is wounded in combat, and he leaves the command of that particular unit. He shows up as the commander of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, as it was referred to at the time, I believe 14 December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let me just go back to the document and ask you about the next line or two. It says: "First offer the able-bodied and armed men to surrender; and if they refuse, destroy them." What do you make of that, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- within a military context, there's nothing wrong with that phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing wrong with destroying the enemy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: An armed combatant, as far as I understand international law, an armed combatant is a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. All right. I don't think I need to ask you about the rest of that directive. Now, let's go to the next document. It's 65 ter 3029, dated 24 November 1992, another document you've cited. This is a document from the Drina Corps Command, dated a couple of days later than the previous one, 24 November: "Very Urgent: Decision for further operations," to the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade Command, personally to the commander or Chief of Staff. It says: "Pursuant to directive of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, strictly confidential number 02/3, of 19 November 1992: 'In an assessment of the situation, I have decided.'" Now, this is a reference to a directive from the Main Staff. It has the same date. The number is slightly different. The one that we looked at was 02/5-10, and this one says "02/3." In your view, what are they referencing? Well, let me not say "they." What is the commander of the Drina Corps, Colonel, at the time, Zivanovic, referencing when he says this directive pursuant to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one looks at the -- the B/C/S version of that document, it says "2-5." So, in fact, he is representing the strategic directive that we've just discussed in the last exhibit. I don't know how it got translated into "2/3," but in the original version, it does, in fact, say "2-5" -- or "2/5."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There's a simple explanation to that. That "5" looks like a "3."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, when looking at an English documents over the years, have you always required to have the B/C/S at hand?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why is that, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I can't claim, by any stretch, to be able to read the language, looking at these documents over the years, the number that I have, particularly those that are written in Latin text, I like to be able to compare the numbers, the military unit designations, because I recognise, from a translation perspective, that many of the military abbreviations and acronyms, our translators don't work with them on a routine basis like myself and the other military analysts do, and it's just a function of trying to make sure that, in fact, military abbreviations, like the 2nd Romanija Brigade or the 1st Zvornik Brigade, get translated properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's just -- I don't want to go over this entire document, but just looking at now in paragraph 1, it says: "Launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up, or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde." What do you make of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a more detailed reflection of the intent that was articulated in strategic directive 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And as we see down in paragraph 2.1, the Zvornik Brigade is given specific instructions or orders, of course, as is the Bratunac, the Birac unit, and some others. Can you, again, very briefly, describe the military situation from this November/December time frame in 1992, leading up to the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Despite the issuance of this order in the middle of November, the VRS, after a few fits and starts, was ultimately not successful in the first month or through the month of December in being able to achieve these objectives. However, at the beginning of January of 1993, they were able to set the conditions and initiate what's generally referred to as the Cerska campaign of 1993. It was a major winter offensive by the Drina Corps which succeeded in two parts. The first part was, you know, defeating the Muslim military forces in the areas that was discussed, in Kamenica, in Cerska, and the Bihac area; and, in effect, also pushing out the Muslim civilian populations who inhabited those areas. The general figures are that half the Muslim population chose to try and go to free territory in Tuzla and the other half of the population migrated south towards the territory under the control of Naser Oric, who was also under significant pressure by the VRS and even some units of the VJ federal army who had crossed across the border to engage in military operations. Many of those people who were forced out of Cerska and Kamenica in January and February of 1992 found themselves, you know, in -- compressed into the Srebrenica urban area when you got to March, April, and May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Really, in the briefest terms you can think of, can you tell us what happened on the ground and especially with regard to what the UN got involved with, just in some spring period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the most detailed accounting is obviously going to be the UN report on Srebrenica, which I think does an excellent job in laying out the background information to that point. But what eventually happened is, as a result of a series of successful VRS military operations, the terrain up in Cerska was liberated. They were able to militarily reverse Naser Oric's gains in the Bratunac area. They opened up the road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac. They reliberated the Kravica village area, and essentially were able to compress Naser Oric's forces into a small pocket centred on the town of Srebrenica. This is what the situation looked like in late April, early May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did the Zvornik Brigade play a role in those military campaigns?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, they did. Their 8th Battalion was particularly active in that area from its base at the time in Drinjaca, as well as other formations such as the Wolves of the Drina, things of that nature. So not only the Zvornik Brigade but all brigades of the Drina Corps used manoeuvre units in order to achieve the necessary military success.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was Vinko Pandurevic in command of the Zvornik Brigade during those campaigns?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He was -- he was in command. Like I say, I believe he assumed command in, roughly, 14 December 1992, and he was directing is brigades military operations at the start Cerska campaign in January of 1993 and throughout the rest of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, just give us the brief conclusion of that story after the Drina Corps was able to bottle up Naser Oric and his forces and the civilian population in this area, what happened, in the spring?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, referencing the UN report on this particular subject, a humanitarian crisis was created because of the upwards of 30, 35, 40.000 people who were compressed into that area. General Mladic at the time agreed to a ceasefire in order to allow for the United Nations to evacuate the civilians out of that particular region. The political leadership of both the UN and the Muslim government at the time, many parties viewed that as the UN being a part of ethnic cleansing, and particularly the Bosnian Muslim government denied permission for those evacuations to take place. At that point, General Morillon, you know, unilaterally declared, you know, the town and the population to be under UN protection, which of course morphed into the future as the UN-protected safe area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't want to get into a lot of detail on all that at this -- at this point or perhaps in the future, but let's go on to another document that you've referred to, 65 ter number 731. This is this publication called the "Drinski," which you've told us is the Zvornik Brigade magazine. Can you just tell us why you've cited this particular area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "Drinski" magazine, as I believe I've testified earlier, particularly at this time, was the monthly military magazine of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. It was published, and, of course, its design was to inform the soldiers of the brigade. It was designed to, in part, help keep morale good. This particular article is a useful -- is a useful history of the combat -- you know, the origin and the combat service, commemorating the third anniversary of the actual creation of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we can go to the B/C/S page 6, so we just don't have the front of the magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps to save some time, we see an article that talks about the leadership of the brigade, then moving in December to Vinko Pandurevic, and then it outlines some of the -- some of the work he had done, some of the -- can you just briefly describe how that -- what's said there, how that fits into your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It reflects, you know, the fact that Major Petkovic, the prior commander of the brigade, was severely wounded. It talks about, in broad terms, the arrival of then Captain First Class Pandurevic as the brigade commander in December of 1992, his work in organising the brigade, improving its combat effectiveness. It talks about, in that second paragraph, the operation lasting from 7 January to 20 February 1992, and the liberated territory with respect to Zvornik and the Drinjaca Road and cutting off enemy forces in other areas of the Cerska region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's go to another exhibit you've cited. It's the next one, 65 ter number 414, and this is a very big document that is entitled "Republika Srpska, Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, Analysis of the Combat Readiness and Activities of the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992." It's dated, in Han Pijesak, April 1993. Now, can you just, first of all, tell us -- and then as we go through it, at the end we see that it's in the name of Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Just briefly, what is this massive document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the professional requirements of, you know, the former JNA and their military education and their understanding of the command and staff functions, in early 1993 the leadership of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska engaged in this study to, in effect, review their performance for the prior year. Essentially, this is their look in the mirror and their written determination of what happened in the course from their establishment to the present, catalogue those things that they have done correctly and they want to continue to expand on, identify those things that they did not do correctly and learn the lessons from that. Essentially, it is a branch-by-branch, department-by-department review that covers all of the functional areas of the Main Staff, starting from morale, going through operations. It talks about security, it talks about logistics, it talks about training, it talks about ammunition availability. It, essentially, is the army's report card of its own performance for the first year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, what's that "ANAGO 92." Any explanation for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you know what that might mean on that front page, "ANAGO 92"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. They didn't translate it, for some reason, and I don't know what it means, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll check that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It also, I left out, it says "Military Secret." Can you tell us, who, in your view, this kind of confidential obviously study would go to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This study was for the purpose of the Main Staff as well as the political leadership of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see, it's page 6 of the English, that the -- basically the table of contents; and then after the table of contents, it says: "Chief of Staff, Major General Milovanovic? Now, this is for 1992 and maybe some of 1993, so I don't want to spend much time on it, frankly. But I do want to ask you about a couple of things that are in here to see if it may have application to 1995. Let's go to the beginning, entitled "Control and Command." It's page 7 of the English, B/C/S page 8. It starts out: "In the past year, the Army of Republika Srpska has evolved into the highest strategic organisational formation of the Serbian people in former Bosnia and Herzegovina, capable of realising the strategic and other tasks assigned to it by the Supreme Command." What do you think that's referring to, the strategic and other tasks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army is, essentially, reflecting, in that line, that it believes it is developing to a point where it is capable and effective in implementing the direction of the Supreme Command, the civilian leadership of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would you include the strategic objectives and the directives in that or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, the strategic directives, as articulated in 6 May -- I'm sorry, on 15 May 1992, you know, are a component part of the strategic direction of the civilian leadership of the Republika Srpska, where they want to take the war aims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It goes on and says: "With its organisational structure comprising seven operational and a number of tactical formations, it is capable of protecting the Serbian people against genocide and of protecting its heritage, of liberating territories belonging to it, and of defeating the Muslim-Croat forces in a significant part of the war theatre." Now, it goes on in one of the following paragraphs. I won't read all of it, but again it refers to "defend the Serbian people against genocide by the Muslim Ustasha forces." Throughout this document, there is references to the Serb people being threatened by genocide. What do you make of that repeated reference, protecting the Serbian people against genocide?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the reoccurring themes, particularly through the public announcements of the military leadership during the course of the war, was that the military operations and the sacrifices that the soldiers were being asked to make were not, in fact, offensive war aims but were necessary in order to protect the Serbian people from the perceived threat of genocide, raising the spectre of what happened in -- you know, during World War II. Primarily, it is a theme that permeates both military documents and also media documents that are for the consumption of the Serbian soldiers in the "Drinski" magazine or in other outlets of that nature. So it is a constant theme throughout the war that, in fact, you know, the reason why they're engaging in these operations is to, in fact, prevent the extermination of their own ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your view, is this propaganda or something else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular document, I don't know that I would call it propaganda, per se, because this is not a document for public consumption. It echoes the theme that I have seen in documents that were for public consumption. So, like I said, I don't think in this context it's propaganda. I mean, the general public is not going to have access to this document; and, therefore, putting it in here for that purpose would be pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving down the page to the fifth paragraph, it says: "During the past year, the Army of Republika Srpska has been under a single control and command structure, despite the fact that initially we had a large number of different armies and paramilitary formations. "This unity has been attained by the following well-known principles, such as unity, continuity, flexibility, efficiency, operationability, and security, with subordination and a single command having a crucial bearing on relations in the control and command process." I emphasise "single command here" because I want to ask you about this. Is this -- is this anything to do with what you were talking about before, when you were getting into the command issues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, these -- these principles of command were not only articulated in the relevant JNA documents on command and staff and brigade command, but you also see these same principles articulated, I believe, in paragraph 174 of the RS Law on the Army. So, again, they reiterate the principles, in part, by noting the fact that it's taken a considerable amount of time in the first year to achieve these particular principles based on what was actually happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page. It's page 8 in both languages; and there, at the top of the page, it says: "Decisions on the engagement of the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska were taken at meetings of bodies of the Main Staff, headed as a rule by the commander, with the presence and active participation of the Chief of the Main Staff, the assistant commanding officers, the heads of the departments, the heads of the combat arms, and a number of operations officers. "The principal decision-making method was the so-called full method. This shows that the situation on the battlefields was regularly monitored and thoroughly analysed, making it unnecessary to apply the fast-track or some other known method." Can you just briefly tell us what you know, if anything, about this full method versus the fast method and what they're talking about here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These particular methods are defined in detail in the 1983 command and staff manual. The full method, in fact, is a comprehensive staff evaluation process, which is the preferred method to want to be able to make key decisions. It allows for the time to study the particular issue, get the advice and input from all of the relevant staff officers and principals so their expertise can be used to the maximum. It allows for the development of various options and plans and decisions as to which particular course of action will be the most effective course of action under the circumstances. It's -- it is the preferred course because, of course, it allows for the full use of the broad range of experience and expertise of the commander's staff. When possible, you don't want a situation where events on the ground are occurring so rapidly that this process cannot take place and your commander is forced to make snap judgements and snap decisions on what are -- you know, could be partial or even erroneous information. So, I mean, certainly this reflects, you know, the significant professionalism and professional education of the army in understanding and knowing this process and implementing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we will get into more specifics, obviously, with the Srebrenica operations in 1995; but as you look just generally at May, June, July 1995, can you determine what method you saw at work during those time periods?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can make a broad statement in that respect. For example, where you had the publication of operational directive 7 and 7-1 and the publishing of orders pursuant to the attack on Srebrenica in July, that was, for the most part, this full method of command and staff analysis. You have a situation on 12 July when, in the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade, the VRS army commander, in consulting with some of his staff officers, not many, but his brigade commanders, makes a much more rapid analysis, assessment, and decision to move on forward to Zepa. So you had examples of both particular decision-making situations encompassed in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll, of course get into that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. McCloskey. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure this is the right time, but I believe there is a problem in translation here. That's why I decided to stand up, because the document is still here in front of us. Earlier on, my colleague read out a portion of the text, ending with the words: [In English] "... and the number of operations officers. [Interpretation] Now, if I look at the text in B/C/S, there's no mention of "operations officers" in this text. Mention is made of administrative officers, officials, but no mention is made of "operations officers." I don't know if the interpreters can be of any help here. The word used in B/C/S is the following: "referent."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can try to sort that out, but somehow I have a feeling operations officers were involved in this military business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't help you, so please go into this during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll work with Madame Fauveau on that and try to sort it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Is there -- is everything okay? All right. Then please try and check with whoever can help you over the break and come back to us later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go much further into the document that starts -- appears to start assigning tasks or priorities. General tasks, I believe, as we see on 154 of the -- of the English. But let's go to 157, because that's where they get to the Drina Corps, and 137 for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what page in the English, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 157. Up there, it's got "Drina Corps." It says: "Task: Shatter, as soon as possible, the Muslim forces in the regions of Srebrenica and Zepa, and then regroup forces and orient at any time them towards Gorazde." So, in April of 1993, when this dated, can you set, again very briefly, the time frame, that this is the task?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular junction of time, VRS army forces are rolling back the Bosnian Muslim forces of Naser Oric in a way smaller and smaller encirclement around Srebrenica, their last stronghold in that particular region. So their goal is to continue military actions against those forces in Srebrenica and Zepa. Then once those military objectives have been taken, you know, shatter those Muslim forces, you know, be able to reorient and begin operations directed against those in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then we see, at the bottom of the English, the date and Dr. Radovan Karadzic's name. Then, if we go over to the next page, 158, it's entitled "Basic characteristics of the operational-tactical utilisation of the Army of Republika Srpska," and it's the same ERN -- it's the continuing ERN series. Then after several pages, this section appears to end in the name of Colonel Dragutin Ilic. Do you know, is this connected to the previous document, in your view, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's connected insomuch as the document signed by Dr. Karadzic is, in fact, incorporated into this larger, you know, army evaluation and study. Colonel Ilic at the time was the chief of operations of the Main Staff of the VRS when this was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know where I believe it was then Colonel Miletic was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe at this time Colonel Miletic was an operations officer on the Main Staff. He was subordinated to Colonel Ilic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's just go in this part of the document to B/C/S page 139, English 160. On the -- well, on the last part of 159, it talks about priorities and discharging set or approval tasks were selected depending on the actual stage of the war. The situation in the various areas of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina," now we're on page 160 of the English, "and general social and economic circumstances." I won't read the rest of it; but if people could read that part to themselves, I just want to focus on this last sentence here: "In the last month and a half, our operations have concentrated on the liberation of Podrinje, as thereby the strategic objective of our war and would be realised, one that could be defined as 'establishing contact with Serbia on the River Drina, or the Drina ceasing to be a frontier,'" quote/unquote, beginning with "establishing." What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an example of how the aims -- you know, the aims and operations of the military were not being conducted in isolation. They were, in fact, being conducted in order to achieve the designated strategic goals of the political leadership of the Republika Srpska, and that ties right back to, I believe, strategic directive 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And on another topic, just the next paragraph: "In Posavina and Western Bosnia, we have put the emphasis on the grouping of forces, air and artillery support; and in Podrinje, in a specific way, the increased expenditure of ammunition and materiel and equipment, as well as the use of reserves of the Main Staff of the Army of RS." Now, this is the sentence I want you to concentrate on: "The presence of the commander of the Main Staff, or a representative of the Main Staff, in the units carrying out the mission of the liberation of Podrinje, is a specific way of giving weight to and steering combat operations towards a single goal." Now, it's very clear what that says and means. This is 1992, right, and perhaps a bit of 1993. Do you see this practice being used relating to Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginnings of the military component of the operation, we see references, I mean, not only to the issue of reporting back to the Main Staff, but, certainly, by the 9th of July, there is a personal -- there is a reference in the reporting to General Gvero being personally present at the IKM where operations are being conducted. Beyond that, even later on the -- sometime during the period of the 10th, General Mladic himself personally shows up at the IKM for the final day of military operations on the 11th, which lead to the capture of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Zepa, any Main Staff person there briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Once military operations began in earnest, and not only military operations, with Zepa there was a concerted effort by the military leadership to try and coerce the political leadership of Zepa to surrender the enclave without military action; and very early on the ground in that effort, Major -- or General-Major Tolimir was present on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about at around the same time with the build-up of forces over in the -- the Croat forces over in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel-General Milovanovic's personal presence out there reflects that same principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's briefly now go to page 162 in the English, page 141 in the B/C/S. There's a bullet point: "By taking Kamenica, Cerska, Glogova, the region of Osmace village, and Jadar, the Drina Corps has considerably expanded the free territory and will shortly have achieved the strategic task assigned to it by the Supreme Command, while at the same time providing protection for the Serbian people." Is this just a reiteration of what you've already said, this document has said, basically, with perhaps more description?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. These are the same terrain features we had been discussing that were involved in the Cerska 1993 campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, I want to continue on in documents that you have cited relating to the RS and VRS focus on these -- on these areas. So let's go to the next document, which is 65 ter 2742. This is from the Army of the Republika Srpska Main Staff. It's now the 1st of May, 1993. It's to the -- to various corps and other units. It's entitled: "Combat order for the liberation of Zepa and Gorazde." It is signed off by deputy command -- deputy commander Major-General Manojlo Milovanovic, drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic. First of all, what significance, if any, is this deputy commander designation of Milovanovic in this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects that for the purpose that this order is being issued, during the time of this order being issued, it reflects the fact that the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, is unavailable to issue the order himself; and, therefore, then General-Major Milovanovic is issuing the order under his authority as the deputy commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this -- and, I mean, we'll get into some of this document in more detail. It's entitled: "Combat order for the liberation of Zepa and Gorazde." Can you put us in a bit of context, where we are now in terms of Srebrenica, and just a very general synopsis of this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects, particularly the first two pages of this document, the understanding of the military leadership of where they are on the ground in the Podrinje area with respect to what they believe the Muslim objectives are to be able to hold on to certain parts of territory, what they think the UN's involvement and actions are going to be; and that based on that particular information, they want to begin to initiate operations to preclude that, specifically as rapidly as possible, to take the area around Zepa and follow on to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But remind us, by May 1st, 1993, is there a Srebrenica enclave, a UN enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a UN safe area designated around Srebrenica. I don't know whether they are calling it the enclave. You know, they never did define the boundaries of it certainly during that period, so I'm not exactly sure of the terminology of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But at that time, would that have been in the mind of the authors of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects the fact that, you know, they're aware that the foreign military intervention under the UN umbrella, and that's how they viewed what happened at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into a little more detail on this. I want to just go to the second page, which should be B/C/S still on the first page, but the second page of the English. It gives a background about the interests of the major powers in the first part. Then it goes on to say: "Expecting more strict sanctions against the FRY and the adoption of the resolution on expanding the mandate of the UN forces from the forces for securing humanitarian assistance to peacekeeping forces, but actually means foreign interventions under the UN umbrella, the enemy is trying to keep the Muslim enclaves in Srednje, Podrinje, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde before the intervention begins, and to take most favourable position on all fronts, especially in Podrinje." Do you have any disagreements with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. That's their point of view of what's happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't know if you can the Muslim point of view, but is that what the Muslims are trying to do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, within the context of how it's discussed in the UN report on the events leading up to Srebrenica, this is exactly what the Muslims have been trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And: "Considering their military defeats in Kamenica, Cerska, and Konjevic Polje, and expecting the fall of Zepa within a short period of time, the Muslim leadership is trying to internationalise the problem of the Podrinje region at any cost by bringing the UN forces to Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde and organising other humanitarian actions which would enable constant presence of the representatives of international organisations in those enclaves." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this is drafted by then Colonel Miletic. In your view, what degree of sophistication and knowledge of the situation does this show on his part?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects a knowledge of both the military situation on the ground in the Drina Corps, and it reflects a broader knowledge of the larger political and diplomatic situation with respect to particularly the United Nations ground forces as well as events that are happening up at the United Nations Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. One last question before the break regarding the next paragraph. It's perhaps the next page in the B/C/S -- well, I'm not sure it is, but it starts: "Therefore, in the following period, the Muslims plan to avoid the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, or overcome their inconvenient operative and tactic position in Podrinje, by proclaiming Gorazde and Zepa 'protected zones,' in order to link these areas and then create conditions for continuing with their attacks, taking over Eastern Bosnia and expelling the Serbs from this territory. "For the time being, they are obviously not able to launch any significant attacks, but we expect sabotage and terrorist actions ... on a larger scale in the regions of Grebka, and they'll try to re-establish the functioning of the Trnovo-Gorazde corridor." Just going through this a little more slowly, "in the following period the Muslims plan to avoid the demilitarisation of Srebrenica," did the Muslims, in fact -- were they able to, in the words of Mr. -- or Colonel Miletic, avoid the demilitarisation of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, I won't get into how -- you know, what kinds of things were taken or not taken, but the Court's, I think, heard more recorded in human history at that point. How about the part about "or overcome their inconvenient operative and tactical position in the Podrinje by proclaiming Gorazde and Zepa protected areas"? Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It did as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "... in order to link up these areas and then create conditions for continuing their attacks, taking over Eastern Bosnia ..." Did they try to do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly with respect to Gorazde and linking it up with the other forces from Central Bosnia, the conduct of the operations out of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves from 1993 to 1995 reflect the fact that while they had combat power to conduct raids and operations of that nature, they were never going to have -- they never generated enough significant combat power to significantly take large swashes of territory that were then under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So then we get the next part "expelling the Serbs from this territory." They didn't get to that part?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not in the -- the area that we're referring to from Zepa to Srebrenica to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were Serbs expelled from the Tuzla area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They were, early in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Completely?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I can't tell you the population numbers specifically, but my own --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think this is military expertise. It's demographic expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was just preparing for cross-examination is all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, let's prepare for the break instead for the time being. So we'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We heard, Mr. President, shortly after your request from Translation, and with the agreement of at least some Defence counsel, that this acronym for "ANAGO" is "Analysis of Readiness."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we're still on the Milovanovic, drafted by Miletic document. I don't want to get into all the ins and outs of that. There's discussions of more Muslim intentions and the Vance-Owen plan and issues, which I don't want to get on to. But on page 7 of the document, in B/C/S, it should be 5, it just lists basically the order: "I have decided the following: The forces of the Drina Corps," with the assistance of various units which I won't get into, and "the support of the Main Staff reserve forces is to crush and destroy the Muslim armed forces in the broader area of Zepa and Gorazde as soon as possible, shall cut off Kladanj-Zivinici road, securing a firm holding of the lines achieved around Srebrenica and on the north-west part of the corps front and prevent the incursion of the Muslim forces from the direction of Kladanj, Kalesija, and Vitnica." It goes on in the next paragraph and gives objectives, one of which is to crush enemy forces in Zepa and liberate Zepa. Was this ever carried out, from this particular plan and this particular time period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS tried to implement this; however, very rapidly, following the creation of the Srebrenica safe area, both Zepa and Gorazde were also declared UN-protected areas as well. So, you know, while preparations were underway to do this, they were never able to actually achieve these goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then going over to page 8, I think it's page 5 in the B/C/S down at the bottom paragraph, it says: "The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska shall coordinate the operation from the IKM in Rogatica. Colonel Dragutin Ilic shall be responsible for merging, planning, linking, and RiK," which means command and control, "of the forces engaged in the liberation of Gorazde and Colonel Radivoje Miletic of the forces engaged in the liberation of Zepa." Now, remind us, at this time, what you believe Miletic's position at this time was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, I believe Colonel Miletic is either the deputy -- I don't think at this point in time he's become the chief of operations. I believe he's the deputy to Colonel Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this sentence is a bit short: "... and Colonel Radivoje Miletic of the forces engaged in the liberation of Zepa." What do you take that to mean that Miletic's responsibilities are, the document drafted by Miletic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, I mean, it's not Miletic being appointed as a commander. What they are saying is, in this -- in this situation, is that these designated officers, Colonel Ilic and Colonel Miletic, will be responsible for coordinating the combat activities from these two various locations. That reflects the practice that we've discussed before, where even though the brigades and corps are conducting these combat operations, there is a preference, where they can, at key locations to have a Main Staff official or officer present at that site in order to de-conflict any potential issues and to continually monitor the combat operations; and if the situation changes, that particular officer is in a position to give guidance as to how to deal with those changes. It is, particularly within the context of the JNA and as we saw it applied to the VRS, a common practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's -- as you've stated, those areas became UN-protected areas. Let's skip ahead to July 1994 and a document that you've cited. It's 65 ter 2667.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just while this document is coming up, I was going to raise this later but there's now an inconsistency. The transcribers have, this time around, correctly attributed that document to Milovanovic. On four previous occasions, page 7, line 19; page 10, line 2; and page 32, lines 11 and 12, they attributed it to Mr. Milutinovic, which might in due course prove confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I don't think the press guy was doing these sorts of documents. I hope not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Back to where we were, we were getting ahead closer to July 1995, but we're still in July 1994, 65 ter 2667, a document from the Drina Corps, under General Zivanovic, entitled "Very Urgent: "Defining tasks from the briefing and urging their completion." It's to the Zvornik Brigade and other brigades of the Drina Corps and some other units. It says: "Pursuant to a briefing on 1 July 1994 to the VRS Main Staff commander by Drina Corps commander and regiment/brigade commanders about level of combat readiness in units and corps commands, pursuant to the tasks issued and pursuant to the VRS Main Staff orders dated 22 July 1994, in order to regulate measures, actions, and tasks relating to the Muslim enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, I am issuing the following order." Then it goes down, under number 1, and reference is by the order of the Main Staff, dated April 18, 1993: "It is now declared null and void (the ceasefire and action around Srebrenica)." What's that a reference to? Tell us about that, just a bit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a reference to the actual ceasefire agreement that was signed by General Mladic and, I believe on the Muslim side, I believe it was General Halilovic, I'm not exactly sure, with respect to the military ceasefire that was brokered by the United Nations in concert with the establishment of the Srebrenica safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I'm not going to go into all the details of that, but there is, I think, one paragraph that helps us understand some of it. It's paragraph 13. It's number 5 in the English. It's B/C/S page 3. It says: "Since Muslim forces and UNPROFOR from the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa did not fulfill the discussed agreement on the demilitarisation of Muslim forces, and since they continued to move around armed and to open fire from infantry weapons and mortars against VRS soldiers and our population, the brigade command (independent infantry battalion) and units and units must take all measures to prevent that and to reduce the enclaves to the area listed in the agreement - Srebrenica town, Zepa, and Gorazde (the town and a three-kilometre area)." What does that document do? What does it tell us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is instructing the brigades to start to enforce what the VRS considered to be the designated boundaries of the particular UN safe areas. They never recognised the much wider areas. You know, they recognised them on their maps as de facto this was the borderline of the UN protected area, but their own understanding of what they had agreed to was that these protected areas would, in fact, be much smaller than the UN's interpretation of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what is your view of what they mean when they say "reduce the enclaves to the urban area"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, with respect to Srebrenica, and I've testified before, my understanding is what the VRS articulated was the one-kilometre by two-kilometre, you know, area that was, in fact, the urban area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What would be the realistic effect of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would be, essentially, looking at the same humanitarian crisis situation that occurred in April of 1993 which triggered the decision to declare the area a safe area in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The statement that I just read out, that they did not fulfill the discussed agreement on demilitarisation of Muslim forces, do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And: "Since they continued to move around armed and to open up fire from infantry weapons and mortars against VRS soldiers and our population ..." Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They in fact did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not going to get into any detail on this, but did the UN provide sufficient forces to protect the Muslim population in Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. They did not, not to protect them in a military sense against an armed aggressor from outside and not in the sense of enough military forces with a requisite mission to enforce the ceasefire agreements or the demilitarisation agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's -- continuing to move towards this, we're now to March of 1995 and documents that you've identified relating to the possible intentions of the RS and the VRS. A document that everyone is familiar with is 65 ter number 5. It's directive 7. It's dated 17 March 1995, under a cover letter from the Chief of Staff Milovanovic, and we see again drafted by Colonel Miletic. As we saw before, there's the listings of the various corps. We get to the Drina Corps listing, page 10 of the English, page 15 of the B/C/S. When it gets to down at the bottom by "Drina Corps," it gets to the area that we're concerned about: "While in the direction of Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves, by planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity, with no hope of further survival or life of the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." Mr. Butler, I don't want to ask you a lot about that. Is that consistent or inconsistent with directive 4, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's -- that's very consistent with directive 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to another -- another section in this. It's page 14 of the English, and it's page 21. It's under this area: "Support for combat operations" under the "Moral and psychological support" area. I believe it's around the fourth paragraph down and it says: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and the humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill, while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." Do you see or infer any reference to the Muslim army in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just how do you -- how do you take -- how do you take this to mean, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it at face value for what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough, fair enough. Let's -- now, after this, which is Defence Exhibit 5D00361, is something called "Directive 7-1", and this is again drafted by Miletic, under the name of Mladic this time. Can you briefly describe to us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a common thing I've seen in connection with some of the other strategic directives, particularly strategic directive 4, where after the issuance of the original directive, the headquarters will issue additional amplifying or technical instructions on how to accomplish these specific goals related to the base directive. What directive 7-1 does is, in fact, lays out a more military technical series of orders and instructions for the corps to implement, so it's exactly clear what they're expected to be able to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are there any references in this document to the two references I've just referred you to, and directive 7 specifically, making life unbearable for the Muslim population, making it impossible, and the reduction of aid to the Muslim population; any references to those two issues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, there are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that -- how does that affect, if it does, those two directives in directive 7?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it does, primarily because the issues related to the control of United Nations convoys, granting the clearance and ultimately determining which convoys will pass and under what circumstance, was not a responsibility that was delegated down to the corps or other formations. It was a responsibility that the Main Staff itself, you know, directed. As a result, given this order going down to the corps giving them more technical guidance and instruction, since they didn't have to deal with that specific aspect of the plan, they didn't need to amplify those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's the issue of restricting. What about the issue of the first one, making life unbearable and impossible for the population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, with respect to this is being a more technical document with respect to military technical tasks, there's not a collateral military order or terminology that equates to -- you know, there's no military mission that says make life, you know, unbearable for a population. You can attack, you can defend, you can advance, but there's no collateral order to say that, so that's not exactly a military goal that can be defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are you familiar with -- well, first of all, are you familiar with a collection of convoy -- humanitarian and UN convoy documents that was assembled by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe that collection and where it came from, as best as you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first few that we had, within the context of the Office of the Prosecutor, was with the seizure of documents for the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade in 1998. There were a number of orders there to the brigade from -- through the Drina Corps to the Main Staff, reflecting what we call convoy clearance messages. Those are messages from the Main Staff sent down to the relevant formations that are responsible for the blockade or the control of convoys back and forth out of the enclave, letting them know which particular convoys and what particular cargo have been approved to go into the enclaves, and which particular cargo and which particular convoys are not approved, and in some cases the circumstances why they were not approved. Bratunac had a collection of these documents because Bratunac controlled the UN access into the enclave over the yellow bridge. Later, as part of the Drina Corps collection, there was a wider selection of these same types of documents, reflecting convoy clearance messages for other parts of the country as well, Zepa, Gorazde, and even Sarajevo, so you just had a much broader framework. But we've seen these documents, from an analytical perspective, since 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And were you asked to review that collection for this testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what were you asked to do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, I was asked to review those documents and present them as a way of providing a not necessarily comprehensive review but give the Court an idea of the types of measures that the Main Staff and the VRS forces undertook with respect to convoy clearance, why they cleared certain convoys and why they did not, what some of their underlying intent and goals were behind these issues, and how the actual practice occurred on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From this collection, did you -- can you in any way tie it to what we saw in directive 7, that talks about restrict -- restricting convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you picked out several.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, I have thought of a way to try do this and save some time, but I -- so I'm going to try to go through these fairly quickly. I just couldn't find a way to save time, and I think it's an important area, given that many of them, as you know, already are authored by General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
