utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you tell us, before we get into the individual documents, what do you know about how this system worked at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, there was a political body of the Republika Srpska that would meet and discuss, in broad terms, issues related to what material could come into the Republika Srpska as part of UN aid packages or UN convoys. It dealt with issues on a nationwide basis, and it was very much involved in ensuring that for aid that was going to the Muslims and to the Croats, that, in fact, the Serbs also received their requisite amount of aid. At the same time, there was a military not body but military officers at the Main Staff who were concerned and dealt with the actual application of the movement of those convoys, designating specific routes, designating specific times, designating specific cargoes; and, certainly, that made sense with respect to the fact that, you know, the Main Staff would have the best view on the ground of ongoing combat activities and would know what areas would be safe for the UN to move convoys through at what particular times. So that particular -- you know, that particular apparatus was in place. Once it was decided which convoys would be able to pass, what times they would be able to pass, what their cargo was, those decisions were then crystalised into orders which were sent to the military units that were actually controlling the access of roads from the United Nations. Convoys coming into Serbia -- from Serbia would either come in through Zvornik or through the bridge at Ljubivoje, so those orders would go there. Convoys going into Srebrenica would go across the yellow bridge, so orders would be sent to the Bratunac Brigade so they could adequately inspect the convoys before it entered the UN territory. Those types of details, and that's how that apparatus worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This political body that you talk about working with the VRS, was there any member of the Main Staff on that body?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was one member of the Main Staff on that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "I believe" --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. My understanding is it was Colonel - and I don't want to butcher the name; I'm not good at it - Djukic -- not Djukic, Djuric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Close enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll probably -- anyway, we'll get to some documents.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That helps. I'm not very good at the names, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've seen the collection of documents that are here. Are those documents that you've identified largely because they were excluding materials, and some other reasons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents that I've selected are there because they show what type of material was included, what type of material was excluded, and also because it gives glimpses into the rationale behind the Main Staff of excluding certain material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And are there plenty of other documents in the collection that you didn't refer to that actually, you know, allow convoys to go through?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct. It's not a comprehensive collection of what I've assembled today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to go through these, and I will probably do some leading; but in coordination with my colleagues, just so we can try to get through them. Let's go to 65 ter 2522, a -- one of these Main Staff -- it's entitled "Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska," 6 March 1995, to the SRK and Drina Corps Command: "In our document of 6 March 1995, we informed you of the convoys and movements of UNPROFOR teams approved for 7 March 1995." Just so we know, this is going to be under the name of Radivoje Miletic, standing in for the chief. In order -- then on page 2: "In order to exercise strict control over the movement of convoys and teams which alone have been approved, we hereby provide details of the convoys which have not been approved, of which you will promptly inform the check-points in order to prevent unapproved movement, as follows." What does this tell us about the process and who was involved in it from the top?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It demonstrates the involvement of the Main Staff in some detail with respect to, again, not only clearing which convoys, but deciding which convoys are not cleared. It shows involvement at the highest levels of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we see this under the name of Radivoje Miletic. Do you have any explanation why he, as it's said here, standing in for the Chief of Staff, why he would be involved in this kind of matter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly can't say that he would have drafted this particular order. But as his role as, you know, standing in now for the Chief of Staff, this was something under the purview of the Main Staff operations people and something that, you know, subordinate staff members would have drafted and expected to go out under his authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he had signed this, would that be significant; if so, how?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how much more significant it will be. You know, a superior is expected to know what orders are being issued in his name. What should normally happen as a part of the process, that even if this is signed for him by a subordinate officer, at some point in time he is expected to review it because he's responsible for it. If he signed it, personally, it reflects the fact that he would have read it, personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Mr. McCloskey. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps it's a technical detail, but I think it's important. I don't believe the document we have here is in order. I don't think it is in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam. Mr. McCloskey, can we see the first page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, maybe you can clear this up for us. We see, in this document, General Miletic telling people to do things, but how do you evaluate that, from his position at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He's not -- he's not directing the subordinate formations to deny convoy clearance. What he's saying, in the context of this order, is that, "We, at the Main Staff, have already decided that these convoys will not pass. We are informing you of our decision. In the event that a convoy shows up at a check-point and is one of these convoys that has already been denied, you're to take the following measures." Those measures are actually explained in detail in following documents, where it specifically notes that, "You're to turn the convoy around and you're to notify the Main Staff." So, at this point, when you look at this document in isolation, you know, there's an assumption that the brigades and the subordinate commands already know what they are supposed to do in the event that a particular convoy that has not been approved shows up at their doorstep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But when he's telling people to do things, like he is here, do you view that as something that the subordinates that he's telling it to have to follow?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The subordinate commands are going to be expected to follow these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't think at this time I'm going to ask you about the standing in for and that whole area. I think that's been dealt with thoroughly. All right. Let me just go to one of the restrictions. It's number 4. It's page 2 in the English. As we see in the top paragraph in the English: "The unapproved movement, as follows," and it describes the Ukrainian Battalion from Sarajevo to Zepa, 7 March, returning 9 March, in order to supply fuel to the Ukrainian Battalion in Zepa. What do you say about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a reflection of part of the larger plan to slowly limit the ability of the United Nations forces to effectively operate under their mandate of policing the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you think of any military reason to prevent the Ukrainian Battalion from getting fuel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only military justification that comes to mind, given the fact that the UN's not going to militarily attack the VRS, would be their suspicion that the Ukrainian military forces in this case might either be providing fuel to the Bosnian Muslim forces or that the fuel that's going there might in some way be hijacked or compromised and still end up in the hands of the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Bosnian Muslims in Zepa, what armed forces were you aware of that would actually use fuel in military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not have military vehicles, per se; it was a light infantry brigade. But there may well have been generators that would have required diesel fuel to provide electricity, things of that nature, which would have facilitated communications. So while they weren't doing large-scale vehicle operations, you know, there certainly would have been a potential for the Muslims to want to siphon fuel off the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next one, 2678. Now, this is one that we should take a look at the original B/C/S, which we see on the screen. Like the other one, it was entitled "Main Staff, Army of Republika Srpska," dated 2 April 1995. Then we have this handwritten part in the upper right-hand corner of the original, which says: "Not a single convoy or ICRC team or MSF may enter Srebrenica without my permission and presence. M. Nikolic." What do you make of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic is the assistant commander for security affairs with the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, which was also the focal point for the Bratunac Brigade controlling the access of material going into the UN enclave. It was an additional -- it was an additional duty he had assigned to him, to perform this function. This is a notation by him. I'm not sure whether this message was actually posted at the yellow bridge or whether it would have been at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. But he's reiterating the fact that before any particular convoy of these natures goes in -- or, you know, to the enclave, he has to personally be there and give it permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So is this -- this original, is that one of the documents found at the Bratunac Brigade, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it wasn't found at the Bratunac Brigade, one, it would be unlikely that it would have Nikolic's handwriting on it; and, second, I kind of recognise the ERN range that reflects the earlier document collections that the ICTY had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can see, on paragraph number 3, a reference to an approved -- I believe it's an approved ICRC team going to Srebrenica. All right. Let's go to the next, 2689.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we see the signature on this document, please, the document that's on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the Registrar scrolls up on the right-hand image, you should -- there it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that the signature you meant, because I didn't understand you that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have understood very well. I just wanted to see the signature at the bottom of this document. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we -- I do want to clarify who's -- what superior officer is at the bottom of each page, and I didn't for that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Butler, can you just tell us on that document, 2678, who is the superior officer whose name this goes out under?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This goes out under the name of General Lieutenant Colonel Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain, they seem to be sharing these duties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a question of sharing the duties, sir, it's a question of, when Colonel Milovanovic is back in the headquarters for any period of time, he's going to reassume his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 2689, dated 7 April 1995, again in the name of Lieutenant-General Milovanovic, and I want to point out the part that's on B/C/S 1. It should be English, page 2: "We did not approve the following in this weekly plan. Material for the Swedish construction project for Srebrenica and Drinjaca on 9 April, 11 April, and 13 April for Srebrenica, until we receive the position of the state for cooperation committee regarding the matter. In addition to the above, we did not approve beef, salt, oil, and clapboards for the enclave on 8, 9, 11, 12 and 13 ..." What do you make of this? In The first paragraph, they're saying, "We didn't approve because we haven't -- we don't have the position of the committee," that I think you've referred to, but then it goes on to say, "but we did not approve those other matters." Can you tell anything about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It reflects the work, first of all, of the state committee. It also reflects the fact that in addition to the above, you know, other issues, these are all -- all food-stuff-related items.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you remind us what the Swedish project is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Swedish ultra project was a project by the International Community to construct temporary housing for Bosnian Muslim population that was displaced back in 1993. I believe they had a construction site going on to the southeast of the town of Srebrenica, towards the -- towards the end of the enclave area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you think of any militarily justifiable reason to not approve beef, salt, oil, clapboards?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The clapboards, potentially, might have a military use; and, again, the food stuffs, particularly within the context of the Swedish ultra project, where they would be under the administration of the International Community, the only potential justifiable reason would have been, you know, a fear that this food stuff might have been stolen by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And his comment: "We wish to remind you that this is the last batch of heating oil being transported to the enclaves as part of the winter programme. According to this plan, our towns will receive 80.000 litres of heating oil and another 20.000 litres of heating oil according to the plan for next week." Why is that referenced there, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it reflects the fact that it's not a matter of generosity that the Republika Srpska is allowing heating oil into the enclaves. It, in fact, reflects the fact that this was a concession that they had to make in order to get their own supplies of heating oil that they didn't have for their own population. So this was reciprocal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one, 65 ter 2687, also 7 April, under the name of Milovanovic. On the first page, it says: "Please be informed that we have not approved movement of the following UNPROFOR convoys and teams," and then it's a list of various places. Getting to number 9 -- sorry, to Srebrenica on April 8th and back on the 9th, comprising seven vehicles and 18 persons which were supposed to transport diesel fuel. That's B/C/S and it should be page 1. It may go into page 2: "We told them that they had 79 tonnes of fuel with Oric." What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's pretty self-explanatory. Their view is that material that is going into the enclave, even though it's supposedly under the mantra of aid to the civilian population or supplies to the UNPROFOR, you know, they're making the case in this context, somewhat flippantly, that, you know, "We're not going to be party for the United Nations to supply our enemies."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Oric have any weapons that you knew of that actually took diesel fuel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe Naser Oric's military forces had any motorised or mechanised weapons systems that would have used diesel fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 10, another convoy related to Srebrenica. It talks about water trailer, field beds, hospital beds, X-ray machine, beams for construction, nails, light fittings, satellite telephone system. I think this is self-explanatory. So some of that can be used for military purposes and some of it can't; is that a fair conclusion to get to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, some of it has potential military utility and some of it is strictly humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to believe that UNPROFOR was providing satellite telephone systems to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not within the -- you know, the aspect of Srebrenica and Zepa. They had already established their own secure communications system. They didn't need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one, 2651A, 14 April 1995. This says: "On behalf of the Chief of Staff Colonel Radivoje Miletic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's just - perhaps my friends can tell me - just the same standing in for and just a different translation. I apologise for the inconsistent translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to take you to page 3 in the English, page 2 in the B/C/S: "We would also like to inform you that we did not authorise the following convoys." Number 1 was one to Zepa involving jeeps and trucks. Number 8 was to Srebrenica, carrying 16 personnel and 17 motor vehicles supposed to carry diesel fuel. Number 9 involves personnel. Number 10 involves personnel and other things. Your knowledge of the investigation, was there any -- was -- did the -- this denying of personnel have any effect on the Dutch-Bat forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In one of the -- one of the actions that was undertaken over the preceding months that seriously compromised the ability of the Dutch UN battalion to accomplish its own missions was the fact that there was a practice where Dutch soldiers who were medically evacuated or who left the enclave for leave or for other purposes were not permitted to return back into the enclave. Those numbers, of course, were always in the fives or tens or fifteens, but over time it created a situation where the Dutch Battalion had a significant shortage of its authorised manpower; and, as a result, it was not able to be -- perform all the missions necessary that it was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to the next one, 2652B, 14 April 1995. This is under Colonel Miletic's name, and it begins by agreeing to several items, including some things to Srebrenica. What I wanted to ask you about is: At the end, I think it's page 3 in the B/C/S and page 4 in the English, and here the document notes that: "This convoy should have taken place on 13 April 1994," I don't know if that's a typo on whose part but, "was unable to pass in Rogatica, owing to our error. We hereby assign the competent person and command to escort the seed programme and for it to take place in full. In the event of any delay and at the check-points, call Colonel Djurdjic immediately on telephone 249." Is this the guy's name that you were trying to pronounce earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so what is this reference of Colonel Miletic mean to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a reflection that the plan to limit the convoys was not just an abstract, and it was not something that was left to other units. There was a great amount of detail placed in the execution of this plan. Those convoys that the Main Staff did not want to travel did not go through, and the collateral was that those convoys that the Main Staff had approved for delivery, you know, there was the same expectation that they would be at the point in time, you know, delivered when they were supposed to be. And in this particular case, a convoy was delayed by error, and the Main Staff, you know, was reiterating back the fact that this convoy has been approved, ensure that it gets to where it's supposed to be when it's supposed to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who is your opinion of who Djurdjic works for, if you can tell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the documents that I see in Colonel Djurdjic is a Main Staff officer. I am not sure, at present, whether he, in fact, worked directly for General Gvero or worked out of the operation shop for Colonel Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next one, 2714, a 2 June 1995 document. This is under the name of Colonel Miletic. On page 1 of the B/C/S, page 2 of the English, it's noting: "We did not approve one truck with school supplies, Karakaj-Zepa," and a listing. "We did not approve 60 litres of oil for saws." As we go down: "We did not approve the Swedish construction project for Srebrenica." Then on 3 in English, near the end, it says: "Note: Persons in the convoy may carry small quantity of cigarettes and food for four days for their personal needs." How was it that we have documents under the name of Miletic controlling actually the amount of cigarettes a person can carry? What does that tell you, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects back to, one, a broader belief that the UN forces were somehow complicit in supplying the Muslim armed forces and the Muslim civilian population with -- by hiding excess cargo or additional food stuff or fuel in their vehicles. It just kind of reflects the specificity of just how closely and how seriously the Main Staff took this particular issue, the fact that they're sending a reminder out to the units at the actual check-point, you know, to ensure these people aren't bringing in food beyond what their immediate needs are or cigarettes for what their immediate needs are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you, as we look through the original, we see this is, of course, like the others. It's like a teletyped format so no signature on it; but, then, at the end of it, we found a handwritten note, which has got the following ERN number, meaning it was somehow connected to this document. Can you connect this handwritten note in any way to this document and account for its potential meaning, where it says: "The RS Army attacked,, we consider that an act of war against the UN and Dutch Battalion," it's in quotes, "and then we want to get in touch with," illegible, "and obtain more information about your future intentions." Then, in quotes: "'Is that it or does your side want to do something else?'" Now, again, in this first document, can you tell if that was that picked up from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I can confirm that because, in fact, on the written notation on the document, when we began our own handwritten indexing, it actually has -- it's my handwriting on the document, reflecting that it's one of the documents I personally indexed out of the Bratunac Brigade. So I know it did, in fact, originate from that location. On a broader level, at the time that this document would have been around on 2 June of 1995, VRS forces were engaged in activities related to the takeover of what is referred to as Dutch OP Echo. That took place late May, early June of 1995, in order to set the framework for future operations in Srebrenica. So reading into it a bit, it sounds like this is, in part, the context of a United Nations complaint to the VRS about those military activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll get into more detail on OP Echo in the future. Let's go to 2717, 12 June 1995, again under the name of Colonel Miletic. It talks about: "The request contains data on unauthorised rotation of personnel. Only the exit of the following persons from the cited enclaves is authorised." How does that fit into your knowledge of what happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's consistent with the practice that I've described earlier, where they were -- you know, they were comfortable letting people out of the enclave, but not putting people back into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then 2497 is an 18 June 1995 document under the name of Colonel Miletic. This one's addressed to the brigades. The part I want to ask you about starts off: "We approved" some UNPROFOR convoys, and then Colonel Miletic says: "I demand a detailed check of all vehicles, including the inspection of cargo. Pay special attention to the fuel and the fuel tanks and the fuel being brought into the enclaves. Check the documents and identity of all persons on board. Make a list of their names and their ID cards in order to ensure that the persons who enter the enclaves must leave the enclaves upon the completion of the task." It goes on: "We informed the UNPROFOR Command about this demand." Now, the Court has seen this before. I don't need a lot of details on what that demand is, but I'm interested in, militarily, we still have Colonel Miletic at this time standing in for the Chief of Staff. What does the fact that he can make a demand to these brigades mean to you regarding his authority, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's reflective of his authority, you know, standing in for the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff. I think this is an accurate reflection of his authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 2551, 29 June 1995, a document again under now Major-General Radivoje Miletic to the Command of Military Post seven11, and it talks about an approved movement of UN civilian observers from Srebrenica to Belgrade. It talks about where it's going, and then it says: "On 29 June 1995, we sent a separate letter to the Drina Corps Command and the Bratunac Brigade-Captain Nikolic, in which we set out the manner of inspection and requests in this connection once they leave the enclave." So what can you infer, if anything, about General Miletic's knowledge or military relationship with Captain Nikolic in this area of endeavour?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're -- they're aware that Captain First Class Momir Nikolic is their point man on the ground dealing with the issue of personnel moving in and out of the Srebrenica enclave. All of that traffic went over the yellow bridge and, you know, the combined UN and VRS check-point at that location. General awareness of the fact that, you know, "We know who's on the ground, we who what's before us," and personal instruction to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 2514. It's a 1 July 1995 document, again in the name of General Miletic, and there's various approvals. I just want to ask you briefly about this one comment. It's page 2 of the B/C/S, page 3 of the English, in the middle. It talks about movement of the convoys, 5 and 6. If you could read that to yourself, it starts with a note. Then, near the middle of it, it says: "If the lorries come to Zvornik without the said cargo, do not let them go to Sarajevo or Srebrenica." He spells it out and says: "In other words, when the convoy arrives in Zvornik, check it, establish what its carrying, and inform the commander, after which instructions regarding continuation of their journey will be given." Do you remember what this is about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is part of what I indicated earlier, that aid that did go into the enclaves in some cases was tied to reciprocal aid that the United Nations or the International Community was providing to the local Serb population; and in this instance, basically, they're noting the fact that, you know, "We're doing an aid convoy into Zvornik. If that convoy does not arrive," you know, "do not allow the supplies to go into the enclaves to follow through."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this case it's not necessarily supplies, but I believe they're talking about personnel rotation, so I just want to be clear, going back to 5 and 6. Medical staff, okay. So they're making -- it's a humanitarian issue, but they're making it reciprocal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Page 28, line 10, it's mentioned "Captain First Class Nikolic." The witness says "Momir Nikolic." It's just that, in that area, Zvornik is mentioned, and I'd like the record clear. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Everyone agrees with that, I suppose. Okay. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Next is 65 ter 2556, 3 July 1995, another one of these documents under General Miletic. It starts out of: "We hereby inform you that we have approved movement of UNPROFOR convoy" number so-and-so "of the Dutch from Srebrenica to Zagreb on 4 July through Bratunac and Zvornik. We have not approved the return of the convoy on 5 July." It describes the composition. Where does this fit in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this point, it's fairly overt. On the timeline for the military operation related to Srebrenica, by the end of June and the 1st or 2nd of July, the Main Staff of the Drina Corps are already into the advanced planning of the military operation against Srebrenica. I believe a warning order is issued on this very -- either on the 2nd or the 3rd. So, you know, they recognise that they're planning, you know, a military operation in that area in the next couple of days, and this is part of the larger programme: Allow the UN forces out, not without a problem, but nobody comes back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next one, 65 ter 230. This is not one of those documents. It's another document that you've talked about in the past. It's a document under the name of Commander -- Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic, dated 4 July, and is entitled "Analysis of Combat Readiness in the First Half of 1995". I just want to ask you about one point. It's in B/C/S page 31, English page 8. It's the fourth paragraph down, and it says: "In the brigade's area of responsibility, a check-point was established for the control of all international organisations entering and leaving the enclave of Srebrenica. This check-point functions in accordance with the orders of the Main Staff of the VRS and instructions and orders of the brigade commander." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How does this fit into what you've been previously telling us about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's an accurate reflection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Blagojevic, is he Momir Nikolic's command at the time of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, Colonel Blagojevic assumed command of the Bratunac Brigade in late May, early June of 1995, so he had been the commander on the ground for approximately four or five weeks when this was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to these -- another convoy document and date order, 65 ter 2558. This is dated 5 July 1995, under the name of General Miletic, and there's one comment at the end of it, when it describes the various approved -- I believe it's approved convoys: "Check them and enable them to travel along the above-cited route. We wish to underline that convoy," number so-and-so, "item 4, must be exhaustively checked at Djuti Most, to prevent photo and video material from being taken out. If you find such material, confiscate it and inform the VRS." Now, in the context of July 5th, what is your analysis of this statement by General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On July 5th, 1995, the mobile forces of the VRS that had deployed to Srebrenica, in order to begin combat operations the following day, by this point of time they would have been approaching their final positions and getting ready at what we would call their jump-off points and line of departure. Certainly, General Miletic is aware of that, and the concern is that they want to make sure that no UN individuals or people leaving the enclave might have taken pictures of these military forces in order -- and somehow, you know, compromised the security or secrecy of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 2570, another convoy document, 18 July 1995. So we've skipped a rough period of time and gone over to 18 July. This is again General Miletic, and it's to the commands of the Military Post Sarajevo, Vlasenica, and Ilaca. It talks about various convoys for other places, as well as number three, which makes a reference to Bratunac on 19 July to monitor medical evacuation: "The following team will travel in UNHCR vehicle," and then it lists a bunch of names. It says: "Note: Related to this journey, security organs of the 1st Bratunac Brigade must constantly monitor their movement and activities. They must not allow them to go anywhere on their own and must restrict their movement, but be very polite. In other words, the security organs must direct their movement." Okay. That's pretty self-explanatory, but why is -- or can you explain, you've got, well, continuing to stand in for the Chief of Staff, Miletic, giving this direction clearly to the security branch. How does that fit into the analysis we've talked about and the professional overview of the security branch, the commander? I mean, this guy isn't any of those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Butler. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, this is a leading question. I am not opposed to the witness explaining to us who this document was sent to and how this document was then implemented. That's okay. But it's not for the Prosecutor to say that these are instructions given to the security organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says it right in the document, but I don't need to quibble over it, over that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we have to continue this discussion, the witness should not be present. But I don't believe that it is for the Prosecutor to interpret this document in that particular manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can respond to that, and it shouldn't -- I mean, just related to this journey, "security organs of the Bratunac 1st Battalion must constantly monitor their movement and activities." All I'm doing is repeating this direction to the security organ. I mean, I don't think that's an unfair conclusion, based on what's in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But was this document addressed to the command of the brigade, to the security organs? Who was it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think we are moving in circles. Let me phrase the question myself. Having read the paragraph yourself, Mr. Butler, what do you make of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sir, it's Colonel Miletic or Colonel -- in this case, I'm sorry, General-Major Miletic, reflecting the fact that while this medical team is in Bratunac, that he expects the Bratunac Brigade security people to restrict their movement, which makes a lot of sense, given the context of what's happening in Bratunac on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was he telling this to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The directive is sent to -- again, within the proper context of the military, it's sent to VP 1111 Vlasenica, which is, in fact, the military command for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can then move to your next question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question is: We've heard about -- is it within the purview of the -- a person standing in for the Chief of Staff to issue this kind of direction?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next one, 2575.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You still have an ample ten minutes for the break or until the break; however, if you -- any time you wish to have the break, please let us know, Mr. McCloskey. It depends on your intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm all right. I got a little sit-down just then, so I think we'll try to get through these documents, if we can. I'm not sure we'll make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But another document, 2575, 20 July 1995, to Military Post 711 and 7590. Again, we're now, of course, beyond some of our dates, but can you -- and this, we see it has to do with the travel of a General Nikolai to Potocari on the 21st, and this is again General Miletic. What events can you relate this to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just this -- this would be reflective of the final negotiations and withdrawal of the Dutch Battalion from Potocari. I believe it took place on 22 or 23 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So this area is a bit -- bit different than what we've been talking about. It's not a convoy restriction, it's not something to do with the security of their forces, it's not something to do, I don't believe, with -- what area, if any, do we see General Miletic becoming involved in now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, again, the withdrawal of the UN Dutch-Bat forces. General Mladic himself was involved with the agreements with General Smith to implement this. This is General Miletic implementing the broad guidance and direction of his commander, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. The next document, 2573. I don't see a date on this. It seems to be a similar document that you've picked out. Anything different to state on that? Again, it mentions General Nikolai.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It reflects the -- it reflects the convoy going in with General Nikolai, and it reflects the convoy clearance with respect to the withdrawal of the Dutch Battalion from Potocari on 21 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And going to 2661A, 26 July 1995, again it's General Miletic involved. And the part I wanted to ask you about is at page 2 of the B/C/S, and it talks about various -- another convoy, a group that was allowed through. It says: "Note: I hereby charge the commander of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade to designate a representative of his unit who will attend the meeting in Bratunac and Srebrenica and follow the movement of the UNHCR team." Can you just tell us what this is about, if you remember? Take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of this message, this is the -- this is the International Community, a series of teams that are coming in, looking for prisoners, looking for individuals that the VRS capture pursuant to Srebrenica, as part of their international duties to identify and catalogue these individuals. And at this point in time, by the 26th, the VRS is now acceding to the demands of the International Community and letting these individuals in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next one, 27 July 1995, and 2586. Do you recall what significance you found in this document? It appears to be allowing Russian soldiers to go on leave --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the significance, the fact that the applications against the UN were not uniform. For the most part, Russian and Ukrainian peacekeepers were allowed far more freedom of movement than Western European counterparts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this might be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. We'll have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Mr. McCloskey, you've asked for 14 hours. How are you doing? Yesterday, you spent three hours and 12 minutes. Today, I haven't made my calculations as yet. But how are you doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I'm doing okay. We get into the minutiae of the documents on the 12th, 13th, 14th, and 15th, and it's hard to say how long that's going to take. I'm feeling it's going to be most of the week. I'll try to -- I'm going to try to get through it, and I will try to cut down also, as I see how it's going, as I do. But it looks like, like I said, most of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm telling you this because you are aware of the filing from the Defence teams about the estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I sure am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, okay, we'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let's go to a few Zvornik Brigade documents you picked out on this same topic of convoy restrictions, the first being 5D00320, and this is a 2 April 1995 regular combat report by Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic. It begins at 0703 hours: "The poturice launched a minor infantry attack." I am not really interested in all that, though I will ask you a little bit later on about this derogatory comment. Mostly, let's go number 10 of this, which talks about UNPROFOR and other humanitarian convoys passing through the border crossing at Karakaj. The last reference is: "An UNPROFOR convoy, The Dutch Battalion, on route from Banja Koviljaca to Srebrenica, two vehicles, four soldiers. They left at 2100 hours on 1 April. One field sterilizer was ceased from the Dutch Battalion." Why did you comment on this seizure of a sterilizer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this context, in a larger sense, it shows that it's not just the Bratunac Brigade at the yellow bridge check-point which is implementing this policy directive against the UN forces in the convoys. It's also the other units as well. In this particular case, you know, my view is that it's hard to prescribe a military or dual-use purpose to something like a sterilizer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next one. It's 5D00321. It's another regular combat report from the Zvornik Brigade under the name of Vinko Pandurevic; and, again, I don't want to get into the military details. But at paragraph 10: "Passage of UNPROFOR convoys and other humanitarian organisations through the Karakaj crossing." It lists a number of those, and then it talks about: "MSF team on the Belgrade-Srebrenica route confiscated the following from this team: Laundry detergent, floor detergent, shampoo, beer, towels, wine, coffee, cigarettes, rolling papers." Why do you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, the same comment I made before. This is a reflection of material that doesn't appear, at its face value, to have any military utility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to another area, getting into some documents I want to ask you about, if they reflect the intentions towards the Srebrenica area, and this would be 65 ter 2920. It's a report from the Command of the 1st Zvornik Brigade under the name of Commander Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic. It's entitled, to the Drina Corps: "The success of our forces in combat operations aimed at crushing the enemy offensive." And if we look at the original, it looks like - as well as the English translation - Drina Corps seems to have written in on top of a line. What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I testified earlier, the practice for a lot of these documents, particularly when they went to multiple organisations, was that they would essentially put the command line, leave a blank, and then they would hand-write in who each of these organisations it went to. So this was a consistent practice with the administrative practices I understand took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm not going to read this whole document, but I do want to read portions of it and ask you about it. It begins by saying: "The moment has come when the issue of liberating the Serbian lands from poturice will be finally resolved in this area by a resolute and successful action of our forces. Obviously, the enemy cannot be allowed to threaten the fate of the Serbian people in this area any more by countless violations of previously-signed truces." Then it goes on to talk about things like media hype. It makes more references to poturice. The last sentence in that paragraph: "One should not be short-sighted and fail to see that, precisely by doing this, they have given us a unique chance to push them away from us for all time, as they are asking for it, and put them under control in this area." Then it goes on: "We must dash for all time their hope of creating a "Muslimanija" extending to the Drina and the Sava, and make it possible for our people to return to their centuries-old homes. It makes more references to poturice, comments like: "The adequate response of our forces meant that we realised that there would be no peace and security in will be in Semberija and Donje Podrinje until the poturice were completely defeated and driven out of this area." What do you make of the messages in this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, the -- this particular document illustrates what, in US military terminology, would be the command climate of this particular brigade. It is a reflection of the views of the commander on a lot of these issues. I suspect that this particular message might have received in -- while it's noted "strictly confidential," that it very well may have been, in some sanitised form, received wider distribution among soldiers and men of the Zvornik Brigade. When -- you know, when I go back to my prior testimony on this issue about command being personal, and those principles of command that were articulated in the JNA regulations about, you know, personal courage, personal attitudes, personal behaviour, and the effect that such behaviour and attitudes had upon subordinates, this is a classic example of a document that, you know, would be reflective of the type of behaviours and attitudes that the brigade commander wanted to encourage through his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But we see in all wars, in fact we see on CNN, leaders making comments of ethnic origin, vilifying people. Does this kind of thing, this kind of example, have, in your view, any kind of a knock-on effect or is it just so much words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is getting so far beyond the confines of this man's expertise. Perhaps we ought to have some foundation if Mr. McCloskey wants to ask him about this document. Does he know who wrote it? Which organ from the brigade it's emanated from? Has he ever spoken to anybody about its contents? Does he know what poturice is or what Muslimanija is. This is way beyond the confines of his expertise and it ought to be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Breaking my question down to its simplest form is: Does a commander's actions, setting an example for his troops, have a knock-on effect on his troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Asked and answered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, in the context of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We got the point. Let me confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Haynes, we have discussed this, and our position is that we don't find this kind of question as necessary for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let's go to the end of this document, where there's a comment that I'd want to ask you about, right at the very end: "Therefore, let us gather our strength with determination and focus it on the most important goal at the moment, driving the enemy away from this area forever and defeating him. That is the only guarantee of our freedom and survival in these lands." About 25 April, can you tell us what, if anything, you know from documents? Is there anything beginning to move towards the Srebrenica enclave, in terms of VRS forces or intent, either before, during, or shortly after this -- this document? Actually, we don't need to go before, I think we've talked about before, but during or after this document, do we see any movement towards this objective of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's an outrageously leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do we see any documents that support this last paragraph of the goal of driving the enemy from Srebrenica? That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's still an outrageously leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not in any way, shape, or form leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the second one is perfectly legitimate. The first one was leading, by all means, but not the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The second one, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Make sure I have them straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, when I'm using the terminology of Vinko Pandurevic, leave that aside.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents reflect the goal as articulated in directive 7; and as we get to the issue of the publication of the combat orders related to the operation directive against Srebrenica, I'm not sure if you see it in such blatant language, but, I mean, those are the military manifestations of this goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let's go to another document that you've talked about. It's 65 ter number 204, and this is a document from the Command of the Drina Corps, dated 15 May, I think, or so after this last one. It is to various brigades, I think all the brigades in the Drina Corps. I'm looking for "Zvornik." Perhaps I don't -- oh, yes -- now I don't see -- I'm sorry. I don't see "Zvornik," but to many brigades of the Drina Corps. It is in the name of Deputy Commander Colonel Radislav Krstic, and I won't ask you about the "deputy commander." I think we've heard enough about what that means. This order is entitled: "Order to stabilise defence around Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves and establish conditions for the liberation of the enclaves." Now, what intention, if any, does the material in this document indicate towards the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by 15 May 1995, the Drina Corps command and staff would have been well aware of directive 7 and the objective that the enclaves were eventually to be taken. They realised that from their current combat positions, that they could not immediately begin military operations with that goal in mind, that there would have to be, to some degree, a series of preliminary orders and operations in order to set the framework for the military operation to actually take Srebrenica to occur. So this represents one of those orders to start taking the necessary steps in order to conduct operations that will ultimately lead to the setting up stage where a military operation against the enclave can be accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to page 2 in English, page 1 in the B/C/S, under the order of General Zivanovic. I won't go into all the details and the units, but it appears to talk about using the forces around the Zepa enclave and talking about Zepa; and then, after that, from there, it goes down and then talks about the continuation of the attack towards the Srebrenica. So what -- in what order is this -- is this plan of operations going, in terms of the enclaves, as far as you can tell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this particular order, it's envisioned that the initial military operations are going to be oriented in the direction of Zepa, as opposed to Srebrenica; and in context of what was happening on the ground at the time, that made a certain amount of sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to document 2892. It is from the Drina Corps Command, 16 May, the same date, "Urgent," regular combat report to the Main Staff. Is there any -- this is at about 6.30 p.m., is how we see it being received from someone, thereabouts. Is there any indication in this document of knowledge of the -- or communication to the Main Staff of this operation related to Srebrenica and Zepa, and particularly looking to the combat readiness status comments on the first page?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It reflects that they're continuing preparation in accordance with "your order."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what's the purpose of the combat report from the Drina Corps to the Main Staff, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the reports, the regular, the interim combat reports, they're a vehicle in order for the subordinate command to keep the superior command informed about what actions are being taken, what the situation is on the ground. It's the report -- the orders and the report phase is part of that larger command doctrine, for lack of a better word, on the issue of verification. This is one mechanism by which the superiors verify that the orders and instructions that they have given are being carried out by subordinates. So reports are a function of verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How important is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fundamental tenet of command. I believe I testified yesterday that orders and directives, instructions, cannot be given in a vacuum, that superiors have a responsibility, under JNA and VRS doctrine as it was applied, to ensure that their orders were accurately complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we'll see -- well, we'll see very soon after this documents coming from the Main Staff to the office of the president in much the same format we've seen the other reports. Do you have anything to add to your analysis for those particular reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, in -- the military was not the only agency that was mandated to report on activities within the combat zones. Particularly by this juncture of May 1995, there was close to if not actually an open distrust between leadership of the army and the political leadership of the Republika Srpska. So in order to ensure that the story and the situation in they were getting of the combat zones from the army was accurate, the RS political organs used the offices of what we know as the RDB, the Republika Srpska internal security apparatus, to also report on actions and activities on the battlefield through the Ministry of the Interior channels. This would, of course, provide the president of the Republic and the political leadership with another source of information by which they could use to verify that what the Main Staff and army were telling them were, in fact, accurate representations of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to 65 ter 205. Now this is dated 16 May 1995. It's a little later in the day. It's about 8.25 -- at some point, about 8.25 is noted in this document, at the end, and it's again entitled: "Stabilisation of defence around Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves, addition to the order." As we go down through it, we see: "Due to a lack of forces to fully succeed in closing of Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves and create conditions for liberation of the enclaves, the above mentioned order is supplemented and changes as follows: Do not perform the planned offensive operations on Srebrenica," and it talks about the units involved,"until the forces are sufficiently reinforced." What does indicate to you of what's going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time these series of orders are going out on the field, the Bosnian Muslim 1st Corps out of Sarajevo is beginning a major offensive in that part of the battlefield. What you see in other documents related to this time is that a number of these forces that were initially earmarked to participate in these activities are, in fact, withdrawn and sent to that more critical sector of the battlefield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want to draw your attention to some map graphics that you've commented on that came out of the Drina Corps collection related to the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, and we'll try, through e-court, to see how this works out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have three of these maps both in full size and in a very simple A3 size, if you would like them. We will be able to see this on e-court, but you don't get the whole picture when you do it on e-court. So we have them here, if you would like them. Counsel has been provided documents in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Have they also been made available to the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, they have. They have full-sized colour copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have full-sized colours, but we have the smaller versions that are right on the top for you if -- that are a little easier to deal with in a courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm told those are the small ones. We have the bigger ones or -- if you'd like them. So the first one, let's see how we can do it with e-court. It's 65 ter 1500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But as we're getting to that, Mr. Butler, we have a miniaturised --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise. We meant to have four, and we do not. That's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have ample time to remedy that by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We certainly will, Mr. President. We may have given the fourth to Mr. Butler by accident. In fact, just to -- all right. There is an English translation version of this as well that people should have, but if we can start with the Srebrenica enclave, like you have, in the centre there. Could we blow that up a bit more. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is entitled, at the top: "Disposition of our enemy and UNPROFOR forces around the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa." If we look carefully at that, we see various markings. Mr. Butler, have you had a chance to look at this document in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to date it at all? Is there any date on this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents are not dated, per se. There is a plan -- there's a comment there with respect to Susica 95, as well as Major General Milenko Zivanovic. So it's my belief that these documents were probably produced originally around March or April of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We haven't got to the documents that say "Susica 95" yet.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This 65 ter is just the one with the disposition of forces on it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, my apologies. Yes, sir. In this context, when you look at the Srebrenica enclave and the Zepa enclave, and the forces that are listed there, they are -- or they fairly well match up to the units of the -- the units and the strengths of the 28th Division and the units in Zepa as we understood them in early July of 19 -- I'm sorry, in early January, February, March of 1995 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what I'm most interested on this document is that we see, in little circles around the perimeter of the enclave, it looks like "UN" is marked in the circles. Have you had a chance to study that and any other materials to determine what those markings mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on this particular map, there, in the lower left-hand corner an English-language translation, it reflects what the symbol is as a UN check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know if that accurately depicts where the UN check-points were in, say, June 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, as far as I know, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you -- can you tell us which one --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go back to Srebrenica for now, really. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell which one of those is, if any of them are, OP Echo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: OP Echo is, if you look --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you're going to be able to mark now. We've got a new system I may have mentioned to you, if the usher could help you. Just if you could circle the mark that you think reflects OP Echo.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you could just put your initials and date it in the right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today is the 15th?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fifteenth.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you had a chance to look at any other documents, UN documents, and compare the locations of the OPs to this map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My primary source of the UN information are those -- those UN documents related to the initial Dutch -- the initial Dutch report on the fall of Srebrenica that's dated approximately 1996; and in that there is a document, at the back of that document, which annexes out what the identifications are of the check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now I want you to go to the next document, which is 65 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please save that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The next document, which is 65 ter 2885. And as that's coming up, I'll just give us a slight -- a short brief on the English. It's entitled: "Drina Corps Command, Battle Plan, Susica." Over on the left-hand corner, it says: "I approve Commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic," but there is no signature. Then on the right-hand corner, it says: "Military secret. Strictly confidential. Susica." It has what the Court has seen before, similar from other maps, the various markings on it, blue, red, red arrows. Can you -- before we get into any more detail on this, have you ever heard of Operation Susica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this particular operation is referenced in either directive 7 or directive 7-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Do they sometimes change the names of their battle plans?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- can you -- is there a date on this that you were able to find?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't believe there's a specific date on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you reference it to any sort of time frame, with your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specifically -- as I discussed before, I believe it would probably have been around the March or April 1995 time frame that the original graphic was created. However, if you look at the area of the Zepa enclave, you'll notice a series of pencil marks. And if you cross-index those between the last series of exhibits we talked about with respect to the Drina Corps in May of -- May 15th and 16th of 1995, these pencil marks and unit designators tend to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just for everyone else, could we bring this up a bit, and right there, and then blow that up, and you'll see pencil marks. You're going to have to go north of Zepa a bit. There you go. That's perfect right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry for interrupting. What do you make of those pencil marks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They tend to correspond with the units identified in some of the initial axes of advance in those 15 and 16 May orders. So it looks like somebody essentially pulled this plan off the shelf, whether it had been approved or not, and very quickly started using, you know, part of it is for the basis of this operation in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just very briefly, I don't want to get into the military manoeuvres, but you know the -- where the attack came from in July 1995. Is this attack plan at all similar to that for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some -- there are some differences with respect to Srebrenica. In this particular context of the way the attack came, there -- more of the forces were on the southern and eastern parts of the enclave. Here they have the attack coming in more from a -- from a northeasterly direction -- or, yeah, from the northwest to the -- to the southeast. Whether it was a reflection of the terrain or whether it was a reflection of other combat forces, they chose to go in slightly different routes in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. How about Zepa, from what you know about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zepa, it is remarkably consistent; and, again, considering the terrain around Zepa, that very much limited where military forces could or could not go. I mean, that's a valid explanation why it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the last map in this series, 65 ter 2884. As that's coming up, this is entitled: "Extract from Drina Corps artillery firing plan towards the enclave of Srebrenica and Zepa." And, again, it's strictly confidential, Susica 95, and it's got target tables and listings and little marks all over this thing. Have you had a chance to review this map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you relate it to any of the -- well, the previous map marked "Susica" in some way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the -- a graphic representation of the fire support plan for this particular operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what are -- can you explain to us -- and if we could -- let's start with Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's blow up the enclave a bit; on the screen, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what these little red rectangles mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those red - those orange, in my case - rectangles are -- they're what are known as target boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you have an opportunity to compare the locations of the UN OPs for Srebrenica and where the target boxes are on this particular map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you find any targeting that was at or near any of the OPs for this plan?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Could you take that pen again and just circle the different areas that you're talking about? Now, I don't know if it's easier for you to circle the target plan or go back to the OP, the UN map.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] I think I can -- I think I can kind of try it this way. This particular location is in very close proximity to what's known as UN OP Mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "very close proximity"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the map distance indicated, within several hundred metres, 200 metres in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you say that, let me just try to clarify it. Does that mean it's targeted within 200 metres or you're saying it's a 200-metre area of accuracy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it is the actual target box itself, some part of that box comes -- in some cases it's on top of, but in other cases it's within 100 or 200 metres of the locations on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This first one, "M," the target box is within how close to the OP, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, it looks like it's no more than -- the OP is no more than 100 metres to -- let me make sure I get this right. It looks like it's no more than 100 metres away to the south and east of the target box.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] This is what is known as UN check-point or OP Alpha; and in this case, it looks like the actual UN check-point is located up on the hill above the town of Slatina -- or, in this case, it's the actual village. The village is the centre of the target box, so this looks like it's 150 metres, 200 metres up the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Any others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] This particular one, I'm not sure what to make of it, because while it is identified on the Bosnian Serb Army map as a UN check-point, and there is a target box within several hundred metres of it, maybe 200, there's no corresponding -- on the Dutch list of check-points, there's no corresponding UN check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't you put a question mark next to that, so we know which one you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Moving further to the south, this corresponds almost exactly on what is known as Check-point Charlie or OP Charlie.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] The last one, I believe it is this one right here, which corresponds to a notation on the artillery map. There's a green flag there with the annotation that says "UN" on it, and it looks like to be a headquarters annotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In July 1995, were you aware of any UN facility in that location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe the UN facility was physically located that far to the east. I believe it was closer to the road at the battery factory complex at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he could sign off on it before I forgot. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please. And while you are signing and it's being recorded, I see next to all these triangles that you were referred to, a reference number, like "122," "342," "340." I tried to see, from the rest of the document, whether there is a table or a legend which corresponds or explains those numbers, but I don't see anything. If you can give us some information on that tomorrow, I think it will be useful. So we stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. I thank you all, and have a nice afternoon and evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of January, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
